title: Hallucination detectivity lab notes — long-context strategies
content:
Purpose: quick working notes for an eval + small experiments sprint to detect and categorize hallucinations that emerge with long-context prompts. Not a polished writeup; mostly hypotheses, short paper takeaways, concrete small experiments we can run on Redwood (hosted and private). Intended audience: applied-ml folks & anyone owning the Eval infra prototype.

High-level framing:
- Problem: hallucination is multi-modal: factual errors, fabrications, unstated assumptions, context-misbinding (answering older parts of a long context rather than most relevant segment). Long contexts introduce new failure modes: stale references, cross-chunk hallucination, leaking of irrelevant tokens into generation.
- Goal: produce a lightweight, automatable detectivity harness that flags likely hallucinations with high precision (we can tune recall later), and gives an interpretable signal for triage (span-level attribution + confidence).

Papers / posts skimmed (quick takeaways):
1) "Contextual Attribution for Hallucination" (arXiv 2028) — core idea: compute gradient / attention-based attribution for generated tokens to input spans and flag tokens with low attribution to the retrieval/context windows. Takeaway: attribute-score thresholds correlate with human judgments of unsupported claims, but collapse on large transformer layers unless smoothed aggregates used.
2) "Temporal Drift in Long-Window LLMs" (NeurIPS 2029 workshop notes) — shows cross-chunk contamination when many similar sections repeat. Suggestion: reservoir sampling of recent context + explicit recency bias in routing reduces drift w/o hurting recall.
3) "Lightweight Fact-Checker: Scoring via Retrieval Consistency" (blog post) — compute a retrieval-consistency score by re-querying retrieved docs with normalized question; hallucinations often have low retrieval-support and low edit-distance to retrieved answers. Cheap and effective as first-pass.
4) "Hallucination Bench: synthetic probes for fabrications" (preprint) — synthetic templates produce measurable PR curves; warns about overfitting detectors to synthetic distributions.

Short synthesis: combine attribution + retrieval-consistency + heuristics (dates, numeric inconsistency) to get a reasonable first-pass detector. Attribution helps localize; retrieval-consistency yields precision; heuristics cover obvious numeric/date errors.

Proposed micro-experiments (can run in one-week sprint):
A) Attribution-probe baseline
- Inputs: 200 multi-section docs (internal anonymized support threads + public docs) with 1–3 question prompts per doc into long-context generation.
- Metric: precision@token of unsupported claims (use small human-labeled subset, ~1000 claims).
- Implementation notes: use integrated gradients-ish approximation or attention-agg (cheap): sum cross-attn weights from last 4 layers aggregated by input chunk.
- Expected: fair localization for explicit copy-based answers; poor for generative paraphrases.

B) Retrieval-consistency probe
- Offline: index corpus (same public docs + internal KB). For each generated claim, run retrieval with normalized question and compute top-k overlap and edit-distance to generated claim (F1-like).
- Metric: binary support (supported/unsupported) vs human labels.
- Expected: high precision on unsupported claims that are verifiable.

C) Combined signal + small classifier
- Combine features: attribution-score, retrieval-overlap, numeric/date-heuristic, token-level perplexity spike (local). Train a small logistic regressor on labeled set.
- Metric: AUC and precision@0.9 recall target.

D) Sanity checks across model variants and quantization
- Run A–D on 3 model variants we serve (base, quantized-8, latency-optimized) to check detector robustness.

Quick tech notes (Redwood infra)
- Use a dedicated lightweight harness route that streams generation + per-token cross-attn probes (we can do approximated cross-attn aggregations in runtime via debug hooks). If runtime hooks are expensive, fallback to post-hoc attribution by re-running with debug attention on shorter context windows.
- Storage: small per-request metadata (attribution map, retrieval hits) persisted in Eval bucket (CSV + JSONL). Keep human-label subset in Google Drive evals folder.
- Tickets/refs: link to ENG-2384 (evaluation infra) and a quick Confluence stub I created (linked_artifacts).

Open questions / risks:
- Attribution signal stability across quantization and compilation kernels. We may see layer-sensitivity; need to standardize which layers to aggregate.
- Labeled data availability: human labeling of hallucination spans is expensive and subjective. Workaround: start with high-agreement synthetic probes + small gold set.
- Privacy/regulatory: internal support threads may contain PII; ensure redaction before using for indexing.

Actionable next steps (next 7 days):
- Aisha/Rohan: assemble 200-doc test set (public docs + sanitized internal threads) — due 2029-10-07.
- Evelyn: prototype cheap retrieval-consistency script (Python using small FAISS index) — due 2029-10-06.
- Me: implement attention-agg extractor in eval harness; if too slow, implement post-hoc using debug route — PoC by 2029-10-09.
- Quick label batch: recruit 2 reviewers to label 500 claims on internal tool (spread across 2 days) — target 2029-10-11.

Possible rapid experiments after PoC:
- Run combined detector across hosted vs dedicated capacity to see SLO impact (latency + cost).
- Evaluate false positives: where detector flags unsupported but human says acceptable paraphrase. Use that to refine thresholds.

Notes to self (random):
- Be careful with heuristics that depend on punctuation; many long-context outputs are sentence-fragmented.
- Keep detector modular: the scoring should be composable so it can be shipped as an optional Redwood Console alert rule.

References / links to read next (prioritized):
- "Contextual Attribution for Hallucination" (arXiv link in linked_artifacts)
- Retrieval-consistency blog (internal link — slack thread #r-consistency)
- Synthetic Hallucination Bench (paper)

End.

MINOR: I used the term "detectivity" as shorthand — we should pick a better name if this becomes productized ("Hallucination Signal" / "Unsupported Claim Detector").
